concept.name: Automated market maker
concept.definition: An automated market maker (AMM) is a decentralized exchange design that replaces the order book with smart-contract liquidity pools: traders swap against pooled reserves and prices are set algorithmically by a pricing function of those reserves.
concept.intuition: Instead of matching your buy order with someone's sell order, the AMM is a robot counterparty that always quotes a price from the contents of its vault.
concept.mechanics: Liquidity providers deposit token pairs into a pool contract; each swap trades against the reserves and moves the price according to the pool's invariant (e.g. the constant-product rule x·y=k in Uniswap v2). Arbitrageurs align pool prices with external markets, and LPs earn a fee on each swap proportional to their share of the pool.
concept.failure_modes: AMM prices only track external markets through arbitrage, so thin or manipulated pools can trade far from fair value; LPs bear impermanent loss and toxic-flow losses that can exceed fee income.
concept.misconceptions: AMMs do not 'discover' prices independently — they follow prices set elsewhere via arbitrage. Providing liquidity is not passive yield; it is an active short-volatility position.
concept.example: In a Uniswap ETH/USDC pool, a trader buying ETH with USDC adds USDC to the pool and removes ETH, automatically raising the pool's ETH price; an arbitrageur then sells ETH back into the pool until its price matches centralized exchanges.
